Definition: Balance or equilibrium — the quality of being well-proportioned, fair, or evenly weighted, in the sense of a diet, a report, an argument, a portfolio, or a person's temperament containing no excessive or one-sided element.

Grammar: Feminine noun: die Ausgewogenheit; usually uncountable, no plural. Derived from the adjective ausgewogen ("balanced"), itself the past participle of the separable verb etwas (Akkusativ) auswiegen ("to weigh out/counterbalance"). Common constructions: auf Ausgewogenheit achten ("to pay attention to balance"), die Ausgewogenheit der Berichterstattung ("the balance of the reporting"), die Ausgewogenheit einer Ernährung ("the balance of a diet").

Example: Die Redaktion legt großen Wert auf die Ausgewogenheit ihrer Berichterstattung. — "The editorial team places great importance on the balance of its reporting." Another example: Eine gute Ausgewogenheit zwischen Arbeit und Freizeit ist wichtig für die Gesundheit. — "A good balance between work and leisure is important for health."

Synonym: das Gleichgewicht / die Balance / die Objektivität (for reporting/argument) depending on context

English: balance / equilibrium / even-handedness · French: équilibre / impartialité Useful nuance: Ausgewogenheit is often used for something that should fairly represent multiple sides or elements — a balanced diet, balanced media coverage, a balanced argument — with a connotation of deliberate fairness or proportion, closer to "even-handedness" than the more general Gleichgewicht, which is the standard word for "equilibrium" in physical, ecological, or political contexts (das ökologische Gleichgewicht, "the ecological balance").

CEFR: roughly B2–C1.

Definition: To enforce, push through, or successfully implement something, such as a demand, plan, law, or one's will (etwas durchsetzen); reflexively, to prevail, assert oneself, or gain acceptance — said of a person, idea, technology, or trend that wins out against resistance or competition (sich durchsetzen).

Grammar: Separable weak verb: durchsetzen – setzte durch – hat durchgesetzt. Transitive: etwas (Akkusativ) [gegen jemanden/etwas (Akkusativ)] durchsetzen (seine Forderungen gegen den Widerstand durchsetzen, "to push one's demands through against resistance"). Reflexive: sich (Akkusativ) [gegen jemanden/etwas (Akkusativ)] durchsetzen (sich gegen die Konkurrenz durchsetzen, "to prevail over the competition"). The prefix separates in a main clause: Er setzt sich durch; infinitive with zu is durchzusetzen. Note: an inseparable, differently stressed verb durchsétzen (past participle durchsetzt, not durchgesetzt) exists with the unrelated meaning "to permeate/intersperse something with something" (ein Gestein, das mit Quarz durchsetzt ist, "rock interspersed with quartz") — a different word from the same root, distinguished by stress and by its participle.

Example: Die Gewerkschaft konnte ihre Forderungen nach höheren Löhnen durchsetzen. — "The union was able to push through its demands for higher wages." Another example: Das neue Modell hat sich schnell auf dem Markt durchgesetzt. — "The new model quickly prevailed/caught on in the market."

Synonym: etwas durchsetzen: erzwingen / durchdrücken / durchbringen; sich durchsetzen: sich behaupten / Erfolg haben / sich etablieren depending on context

English: to enforce / to push through / to implement; sich durchsetzen: to prevail / to assert oneself / to win out · French: imposer / faire valoir; sich durchsetzen: s'imposer / l'emporter Useful nuance: Durchsetzen (transitive) emphasizes successfully making something happen despite obstacles or opposition — a policy, a demand, one's will. Sich durchsetzen (reflexive) shifts the focus to a person, idea, or product itself winning out or gaining acceptance, often in competition with alternatives. Don't confuse either with sich einsetzen [für etwas] ("to advocate/campaign for something"), which describes effort toward a goal without necessarily implying success.

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: To dissuade or talk someone out of doing something, or to divert someone from a plan, opinion, or course of action, usually through persuasion or argument.

Grammar: Separable strong verb: abbringen – brachte ab – hat abgebracht. Construction: jemanden (Akkusativ) von etwas (Dativ) abbringen (ihn von seinem Plan abbringen, "to talk him out of his plan"). Often used in the negative to express that someone cannot be dissuaded: sich von etwas nicht abbringen lassen ("to not let oneself be talked out of something"). The prefix separates in a main clause: Sie bringt ihn davon ab; infinitive with zu is abzubringen.

Example: Seine Freunde konnten ihn nicht von seinem Vorhaben abbringen. — "His friends could not talk him out of his plan." Another example: Sie ließ sich von niemandem von ihrer Meinung abbringen. — "She would not let anyone talk her out of her opinion."

Synonym: jemanden von etwas überzeugen, es nicht zu tun / jemandem etwas ausreden / jemanden umstimmen depending on context

English: to dissuade / to talk out of / to divert from · French: dissuader / détourner de Useful nuance: Abbringen always specifies what someone is being diverted from with von + Dativ — a plan, a decision, an opinion, a path. The common construction sich nicht abbringen lassen ("to not be dissuaded/deterred") emphasizes stubborn resolve. It contrasts with überreden ("to persuade someone to do something"), which points the other direction.

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: Deliberate, careful, and unhurried in manner, thought, speech, or movement — thinking things through before acting or speaking, often at a measured, slow pace. Depending on context it can sound either positive (thoughtful, prudent) or mildly critical (overly slow, ponderous).

Grammar: Adjective, also used adverbially: eine bedächtige Antwort, Er sprach bedächtig. Regular inflection before a noun according to case, gender, number, and determiner: bedächtig, bedächtiger, am bedächtigsten. Related to the verb bedenken ("to consider, think over") and the adjective bedacht ("mindful, careful," often in auf etwas (Akkusativ) bedacht sein, "to be intent on/mindful of something").

Example: Der alte Mann ging langsam und bedächtig über den Hof. — "The old man walked slowly and deliberately across the yard." Another example: Sie antwortete bedächtig, nachdem sie kurz nachgedacht hatte. — "She answered thoughtfully, after considering briefly."

Synonym: besonnen / überlegt / bedachtsam / langsam und überlegt depending on context

English: deliberate / thoughtful / measured / unhurried · French: posé / réfléchi / mesuré Useful nuance: Bedächtig emphasizes a slow, considered manner — someone who thinks before acting or speaking, whether admiringly ("prudent, careful") or with a hint of impatience ("ponderous, slow"). Besonnen leans more purely positive, stressing level-headedness and composure, especially in a crisis, while bedächtig more strongly evokes physical or verbal slowness alongside the thoughtfulness.

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: To withdraw, take away, or revoke something from someone — a right, license, privilege, trust, or, as in the sample phrase um ihm seine Verantwortung zu entziehen ("in order to relieve/strip him of his responsibility"), a duty or area of authority. Reflexively, sich (Dativ) etwas entziehen or sich einer Sache (Dativ) entziehen means to withdraw oneself from something, to evade or escape it (a duty, judgment, someone's grasp or view).

Grammar: Strong, inseparable verb: entziehen – entzog – hat entzogen. Construction: jemandem (Dativ) etwas (Akkusativ) entziehen (ihm seine Verantwortung entziehen, "to relieve him of his responsibility"; jemandem die Fahrerlaubnis entziehen, "to revoke someone's driving license"). Reflexive: sich (Dativ) etwas (Dativ) entziehen (sich der Verantwortung entziehen, "to evade responsibility"; sich jemandes Blicken entziehen, "to withdraw from someone's gaze"). Related noun: der Entzug ("withdrawal," also used for medical detox: der Drogenentzug).

Example: Der Vorstand beschloss, ihm seine Verantwortung zu entziehen und sie einem anderen Kollegen zu übertragen. — "The board decided to relieve him of his responsibility and hand it to another colleague." Another example: Sie versuchte, sich ihrer Verantwortung zu entziehen, indem sie die Schuld auf andere schob. — "She tried to evade her responsibility by shifting the blame onto others."

Synonym: jemandem etwas wegnehmen / jemandem etwas aberkennen / jemandem etwas nehmen depending on context; reflexively sich einer Sache entziehen: sich einer Sache entwinden / sich einer Sache entziehen/ausweichen

English: to withdraw / to take away / to revoke / to deprive of; reflexively to evade / to escape / to withdraw from · French: retirer / priver de / soustraire; se soustraire à Useful nuance: The dative person and accusative thing pattern (jemandem etwas entziehen) marks who loses something and what is taken; it's the standard verb for formally revoking a license, right, or area of authority. The reflexive sich einer Sache entziehen flips the direction — the subject actively withdraws from or dodges an obligation, scrutiny, or grasp, closer to "evade" than to being deprived of something.

CEFR: roughly B2–C1.

Definition: Effort, dedication, or commitment put into an activity — as in the sample phrase mit vollem Einsatz dabei sein ("to be fully committed/giving it one's all"). The word has several other common senses: the deployment or use of resources, personnel, or equipment (der Einsatz von Personal, "the deployment of staff"); a mission or operation, especially military or emergency-service (im Einsatz sein, "to be on duty/deployed"); a stake or bet in gambling; and, in music, the entrance or cue for a voice or instrument to begin.

Grammar: Masculine noun: der Einsatz; plural: die Einsätze. Derived from the separable verb etwas (Akkusativ) einsetzen ("to deploy, use, insert") and reflexive sich (Akkusativ) [für jemanden/etwas (Akkusativ)] einsetzen ("to commit oneself/advocate for someone or something"). Common constructions: mit vollem Einsatz ("with full commitment/effort"), im Einsatz sein ("to be deployed/on duty"), seinen Einsatz zeigen ("to show one's commitment"), and unter Einsatz seines Lebens ("at the risk of one's life").

Example: Die Mannschaft war den ganzen Abend mit vollem Einsatz dabei. — "The team was fully committed all evening, giving it everything." Another example: Die Feuerwehr war schon wenige Minuten nach dem Alarm im Einsatz. — "The fire department was already on the scene/deployed just a few minutes after the alarm."

Synonym: effort/commitment sense: die Hingabe / das Engagement / die Anstrengung; deployment sense: die Verwendung / der Gebrauch; mission sense: der Auftrag / die Mission depending on context

English: effort / commitment / dedication; also deployment / use / mission / stake (gambling) / entrance (music) · French: engagement / dévouement; aussi déploiement / usage / mission / mise Useful nuance: In the phrase mit vollem Einsatz, Einsatz describes the visible energy and dedication someone puts into a task or competition, similar to English "giving it your all." This sense is closely tied to the reflexive verb sich einsetzen ("to commit oneself to something") — someone who shows Einsatz is someone who sich einsetzt. Context determines which of the word's several meanings (effort, deployment, stake, musical entrance) applies.

CEFR: roughly B1–B2.

Definition: Supplies, reinforcements, or fresh stock brought in to replenish what has been used up — originally and still commonly a military term for the resupply of troops with matériel, ammunition, or provisions, but also used more broadly and colloquially for replenishing any resource (food, goods, coffee, etc.).

Grammar: Masculine noun: der Nachschub; usually uncountable, no plural. Derived from the separable verb etwas (Akkusativ) nachschieben ("to push/supply something afterward"). Common constructions: Nachschub an etwas (Dativ) (Nachschub an Munition, "a resupply of ammunition"), Nachschub bekommen/ brauchen ("to get/need fresh supplies"), and für Nachschub sorgen ("to see to resupply/restocking"). Related to [[der Tross]] (a baggage/supply train).

Example: Die eingeschlossenen Truppen warteten dringend auf Nachschub an Lebensmitteln und Munition. — "The besieged troops were urgently waiting for a resupply of food and ammunition." Another example: Kannst du beim Einkaufen gleich Nachschub an Kaffee besorgen? — "Can you pick up more coffee while you're shopping?"

Synonym: die Versorgung / der Nachschubdienst / die Nachlieferung depending on context

English: supplies / resupply / reinforcements / fresh stock · French: ravitaillement / réserves Useful nuance: Nachschub keeps a military or logistical flavor even in its colloquial extensions — using it for coffee or snacks running low has a slightly jokey, mock-serious tone, as if treating the household supply like a military resupply operation. Versorgung is the more neutral, general word for "supply/ provisioning."

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: Moderation or restraint — the quality or act of keeping something (behavior, consumption, emotions, demands) within reasonable, measured limits rather than excessive or extreme; also used in political/diplomatic contexts for a policy of restraint or conciliation toward an opposing side.

Grammar: Feminine noun: die Mäßigung; usually uncountable, no plural. Derived from the verb etwas (Akkusativ) mäßigen ("to moderate/temper something") and reflexive sich (Akkusativ) mäßigen ("to restrain/moderate oneself"). Common constructions: zur Mäßigung aufrufen ("to call for restraint/ moderation"), Mäßigung üben ("to exercise restraint"), and mit Mäßigung ("with moderation").

Example: Die Regierung rief beide Seiten zur Mäßigung auf. — "The government called on both sides to exercise restraint." Another example: Er isst und trinkt immer mit Mäßigung. — "He always eats and drinks in moderation."

Synonym: die Zurückhaltung / die Beherrschung / das Maßhalten depending on context; opposite: die Maßlosigkeit / der Exzess

English: moderation / restraint / temperance · French: modération / retenue Useful nuance: Mäßigung often appears in political and diplomatic register (zur Mäßigung aufrufen, calling on parties in a conflict to show restraint), giving it a more formal, public tone than the everyday Zurückhaltung ("restraint/reserve," more personal). The related reflexive verb sich mäßigen is common in everyday advice, e.g. telling someone to calm down or moderate their behavior.

CEFR: roughly C1.

Definition: Moderate, measured, or restrained — describing behavior, demands, tone, or actions that stay within sensible, appropriate limits rather than being excessive, extreme, or exaggerated.

Grammar: Adjective, regular declension: maßvoll, maßvolle, maßvoller, maßvolles. Formed from das Maß ("measure/moderation") + -voll ("full of"), literally "full of measure." Common constructions: maßvolle Kritik ("measured criticism"), maßvoll reagieren ("to react moderately/with restraint"), and eine maßvolle Lohnerhöhung ("a moderate pay raise").

Example: Die Opposition übte maßvolle Kritik an der Reform. — "The opposition offered measured criticism of the reform." Another example: Er reagierte auch in der hitzigen Debatte maßvoll und sachlich. — "Even in the heated debate, he reacted moderately and matter-of-factly."

Synonym: gemäßigt / zurückhaltend / besonnen depending on context; opposite: maßlos / übertrieben / exzessiv

English: moderate / measured / restrained · French: modéré / mesuré Useful nuance: maßvoll is closely related to [[die Mäßigung]] and the verb sich mäßigen — where Mäßigung names the quality or act of restraint, maßvoll describes something (a reaction, a demand, a tone) that displays that quality. It's often used approvingly, especially in political or journalistic writing, to praise a response as sensible and proportionate rather than inflammatory.

CEFR: roughly C1.

Definition: Effort or exertion — the physical or mental energy expended to achieve something difficult or demanding; can refer to a single effort/endeavor or, in the plural, to sustained efforts/pains taken toward a goal.

Grammar: Feminine noun: die Anstrengung; plural: die Anstrengungen. Derived from the reflexive verb sich (Akkusativ) anstrengen ("to exert oneself, make an effort") and transitive etwas (Akkusativ) anstrengen ("to strain/tax something," e.g. die Augen anstrengen, "to strain one's eyes"). Common constructions: Anstrengungen unternehmen ("to make efforts"), unter großer Anstrengung ("with great effort/exertion"), and es ist der Anstrengung wert ("it's worth the effort").

Example: Trotz aller Anstrengungen konnte die Mannschaft die Niederlage nicht verhindern. — "Despite all efforts, the team could not prevent the defeat." Another example: Das lange Bergwandern war eine echte körperliche Anstrengung. — "The long mountain hike was a real physical exertion."

Synonym: die Mühe / der Aufwand / die Bemühung depending on context; intensified: die Kraftanstrengung ("major effort/exertion")

English: effort / exertion / strain · French: effort / peine Useful nuance: Anstrengung leans toward the effortful, taxing side of exertion — physical strain, mental concentration, or sustained endeavor — and pairs naturally with groß, körperlich, geistig ("great, physical, mental"). It differs from [[der Einsatz]], which emphasizes visible commitment/dedication (as in sport or duty) rather than the sheer exertion or strain involved.

CEFR: roughly B1/B2.

Definition: Zeal, ardor, or eagerness — enthusiastic, energetic dedication to a task, cause, or goal, often with a connotation of impatience or excessive keenness; can be positive (diligent enthusiasm) or slightly critical (overzealousness).

Grammar: Masculine noun: der Eifer; uncountable, no plural. Related adjective: eifrig ("eager, zealous, diligent"). Common constructions: mit Eifer bei der Sache sein ("to be zealously engaged in something"), im Eifer des Gefechts ("in the heat of the moment," literally "in the zeal of battle"), and blinder Eifer ("blind zeal," i.e. overenthusiasm that does more harm than good).

Example: Sie stürzte sich mit großem Eifer in die neue Aufgabe. — "She threw herself into the new task with great zeal." Another example: Im Eifer des Gefechts hatte er ganz vergessen, die Tür abzuschließen. — "In the heat of the moment, he had completely forgotten to lock the door."

Synonym: die Begeisterung / der Elan / die Inbrunst depending on context; overzealous sense: der Übereifer

English: zeal / ardor / eagerness / fervor · French: zèle / ardeur / empressement Useful nuance: Eifer sits close to [[die Anstrengung]] and [[der Einsatz]] but names the emotional drive/enthusiasm behind an effort rather than the exertion or commitment itself. The idiom im Eifer des Gefechts is very common for describing something said or done hastily amid excitement or heated activity, and blinder Eifer captures the specifically German-flavored caution that overzealousness can backfire — echoed in the proverb "blinder Eifer schadet nur" ("blind zeal only does harm").

CEFR: roughly B2/C1.

Definition: To keep oneself from (doing) something, to refrain — the reflexive counterpart of jemanden davon abhalten ("to keep/prevent someone from doing something"); davon is a pronominal adverb pointing forward or back to an infinitive clause (..., etwas zu tun), so sich davon abhalten literally means "to hold oneself back from that [action]."

Grammar: Separable strong verb: abhalten, hielt ab, hat abgehalten. Base transitive construction: jemanden (Akkusativ) von etwas/davon (+ zu-Infinitiv) abhalten (ihn davon abhalten, zu gehen, "to keep him from leaving"). Reflexive: sich (Akkusativ) von etwas/davon abhalten [lassen] — used almost always with a modal (lassen, können) rather than as a bare main verb: sich davon abhalten lassen ("to let oneself be kept/deterred from it") or, in the negative, sich davon nicht abhalten lassen ("to not let anything stop one"). The davon stands in for a zu-infinitive clause that follows or was just mentioned (..., davon abzuhalten, etwas zu tun). The prefix separates in a main clause: Sie hält sich davon ab; infinitive with zu is abzuhalten.

Example: Lass dich nicht davon abhalten, deine Ziele zu verfolgen. — "Don't let yourself be kept from pursuing your goals." Another example: Er konnte sich nicht davon abhalten, ständig aufs Handy zu schauen. — "He couldn't stop himself from constantly checking his phone."

Synonym: sich zurückhalten / sich etwas verkneifen / auf etwas verzichten depending on context; opposite construction: sich nicht abhalten lassen ("to not let oneself be stopped/deterred")

English: to keep oneself from / to refrain from / (with lassen) to let oneself be deterred from · French: se retenir de / s'empêcher de Useful nuance: In practice, sich davon abhalten rarely stands alone as a plain reflexive verb; it almost always appears with lassen (sich davon abhalten lassen, "to let oneself be deterred/kept from it"), especially in the negative imperative or statement of resolve (lass dich nicht davon abhalten..., sie ließ sich nicht davon abhalten...). Compare the transitive jemanden davon abhalten, where one person actively stops another — the reflexive shifts this to stopping (or failing to stop) oneself.

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: To awaken or arouse — literally, to rouse someone from sleep or, in elevated/literary use, to bring back to life (zum Leben erwecken); much more commonly used figuratively, to evoke or give rise to a feeling, interest, or impression, especially in the fixed phrase den Eindruck erwecken, dass... ("to create/ give the impression that...").

Grammar: Weak, inseparable verb: erwecken, erweckte, hat erweckt. Governs the accusative: etwas/ jemanden (Akkusativ) erwecken. Key fixed constructions: den Eindruck erwecken, dass... ("to give the impression that..."), Interesse/Aufmerksamkeit erwecken ("to arouse interest/attention"), Hoffnungen erwecken ("to raise hopes"), jemanden/etwas zum Leben erwecken ("to bring someone/something to life," literal in fiction/myth or figurative for a project, character, city district, etc.). Related noun: die Erweckung ("awakening," also religious, as in die Erweckungsbewegung, "revivalist movement").

Example: Seine Rede erweckte den Eindruck, dass er die Entscheidung bereits getroffen hatte. — "His speech gave the impression that he had already made the decision." Another example: Die alte Fabrikhalle wurde durch das neue Kulturzentrum wieder zum Leben erweckt. — "The old factory hall was brought back to life by the new cultural center."

Synonym: wecken (the everyday, non-figurative counterpart) · hervorrufen / auslösen (evoke/trigger, for feelings or reactions) · zum Leben erwecken: wiederbeleben (revive) depending on context

English: to awaken / arouse / evoke; (den Eindruck erwecken) to give the impression · French: éveiller / susciter; donner l'impression Useful nuance: erwecken sits a register above plain wecken ("to wake someone up," e.g. with an alarm clock) and is reserved for figurative, literary, or elevated contexts — impressions, feelings, interest, hopes, or a dramatic "return to life." The idiom den Eindruck erwecken, dass... is extremely common in news and formal writing as a slightly more cautious/distancing way to report something than stating it as fact outright (implying "it seems/appears that," without fully committing).

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: As a verb, verderben means to spoil or go bad (food, transitively or intransitively), to ruin or spoil something (a mood, an occasion, a plan), or to corrupt someone morally; the past participle verdorben also functions as an adjective ("spoiled, rotten; morally corrupt/depraved"). As a nominalized infinitive, das Verderben is a more literary/dramatic noun meaning ruin, doom, or perdition — utter downfall or destruction, often in a fateful sense.

Grammar: Strong, irregular verb: verderben, verdarb, hat/ist verdorben — intransitive with sein when describing something going bad itself (die Milch ist verdorben, "the milk has gone bad"), transitive with haben when someone/something spoils or ruins something else (er hat mir den Abend verdorben, "he ruined my evening" — dative of the person affected + accusative of the thing ruined). Common fixed constructions: jemandem die Laune/den Tag/den Spaß verderben ("to ruin someone's mood/day/fun"), sich (Dativ) den Magen verderben ("to upset one's stomach"), es sich mit jemandem verderben ("to fall out of favor with someone, spoil one's relationship with someone"). The adjective verdorben declines regularly: verdorbene Lebensmittel ("spoiled food"), ein verdorbener Charakter ("a corrupt/depraved character"). The nominalized das Verderben is uncountable, usually appearing in phrases like jemanden ins Verderben stürzen/reißen ("to plunge/drag someone into ruin") and sein eigenes Verderben ("one's own downfall/undoing").

Example: Die Hitze hat das Fleisch schnell verderben lassen. — "The heat quickly caused the meat to spoil." Another example: Seine Gier stürzte ihn schließlich ins Verderben. — "His greed ultimately plunged him into ruin."

Synonym: verderben (spoil food): schlecht werden / faulen; verderben (ruin something): ruinieren / vermiesen / kaputtmachen; verderben (corrupt someone): korrumpieren; das Verderben: der Untergang / der Ruin / das Unheil depending on context

English: verderben: to spoil / go bad / ruin; to corrupt; verdorben: spoiled, corrupt/depraved; das Verderben: ruin / doom / perdition · French: verderben: gâter / pourrir; corrompre; das Verderben: perte / perdition / ruine Useful nuance: The everyday senses of verderben (spoiled milk, a ruined mood, an upset stomach) feel quite mundane, but the nominalized das Verderben keeps a heightened, almost biblical or tragic register — it's the word used for a fateful, often self-inflicted downfall (sein eigenes Verderben, ins Verderben stürzen), closer to English "doom/perdition" than to the plain verb's "spoil/ruin." Don't confuse verderben with verderblich ("perishable," as in verderbliche Lebensmittel, "perishable food").

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: To lend out or rent out something (a physical item, for temporary use, typically for a fee); or, figuratively, to confer, bestow, or award something abstract — a prize, title, honor, or quality/characteristic — onto someone or something.

Grammar: Strong, inseparable verb: verleihen, verlieh, hat verliehen. Governs dative of recipient + accusative of the thing given: jemandem etwas (Akkusativ) verleihen. Common fixed constructions: einen Preis/Titel/Orden verleihen ("to award a prize/title/medal"), einer Sache (Dativ) Ausdruck verleihen ("to give expression to something," e.g. a feeling), jemandem Kraft/Mut verleihen ("to give someone strength/courage," often figuratively), and, literally, Fahrräder/Bücher verleihen ("to rent out bikes/lend out books"). Related nouns: die Verleihung ("the awarding, presentation ceremony," e.g. die Oscar-Verleihung), and der Verleih ("a rental business or distribution agency," e.g. der Fahrradverleih, "bike rental," der Filmverleih, "film distribution company").

Example: Der Nobelpreis wird jedes Jahr in Stockholm verliehen. — "The Nobel Prize is awarded every year in Stockholm." Another example: Die ruhige Musik verleiht dem Film eine besondere Atmosphäre. — "The calm music lends the film a special atmosphere."

Synonym: lending sense: ausleihen / vermieten (for a fee); conferring sense: vergeben / zuerkennen (award) / geben (give, more general) depending on context

English: to lend/rent out; to confer/bestow/award · French: prêter/louer; conférer/décerner Useful nuance: The figurative sense (einer Sache Ausdruck/Kraft/eine Atmosphäre verleihen) is extremely common in written and journalistic German for describing how one thing imparts a quality to another — a piece of music lending a film atmosphere, a gesture lending words emphasis — functioning much like English "lend" in "lends credibility to." Don't confuse it with ausleihen (to borrow/check out, from the borrower's perspective) — verleihen is always from the giver's/lender's side.

CEFR: roughly B2.

Definition: Concern, worry, or apprehension — a formal noun for unease about a potential negative development or outcome, often used in news, official, or medical/diagnostic register rather than everyday speech.

Grammar: Feminine noun: die Besorgnis; plural die Besorgnisse (uncommon, mostly used in singular). Related adjective besorgt ("worried, concerned"), and the compound adjective besorgniserregend ("alarming, worrying," literally "concern-arousing" — see [[erwecken]]/erregen). Common fixed constructions: Anlass zur Besorgnis geben ("to give cause for concern"), mit [wachsender] Besorgnis ("with [growing] concern"), Besorgnis äußern ("to express concern"), etwas erfüllt jemanden mit Besorgnis ("something fills someone with concern").

Example: Der starke Anstieg der Fälle gibt Anlass zur Besorgnis. — "The sharp rise in cases gives cause for concern." Another example: Die Ärzte äußerten Besorgnis über den Gesundheitszustand des Patienten. — "The doctors expressed concern about the patient's state of health."

Synonym: die Sorge (more everyday/general worry) · die Beunruhigung (unease, disquiet) · die Befürchtung (a specific fear/apprehension that something will happen) depending on context

English: concern / worry / apprehension · French: inquiétude / préoccupation Useful nuance: Besorgnis is a notably formal, written-register word — common in news reports, official statements, and medical contexts (Anlass zur Besorgnis, besorgniserregender Zustand, "an alarming/ worrying condition") — where everyday spoken German would simply use Sorge or Angst. The derived adjective besorgniserregend is extremely common in journalism for describing statistics, trends, or situations that are cause for alarm.

CEFR: roughly B2/C1.
